title: This 9-Year-Old Collects Vintage Toilets — and Dreams of Designing Them
summary:
Most 9-year-olds collect trading cards or toy cars. Damian Skaer collects toilets — about 40 of them.

Damian, who lives in Eastern Washington, first fell in love with toilets by watching plumbers on YouTube. In the videos, workers replace, test, and fix toilets — and Damian was hooked. His dad, Roger Skaer, says Damian is fascinated by the engineering behind toilets.

Damian's collection started with a couple of old toilets he found in his grandparents' barn. Since then, it has grown to about 40. They include a pale yellow 1965 American Standard Cadet, a robin's-egg-blue 1963 Crane Oxford, and a 1972 Kohler Wellworth the color of an army tank. They stand on an 11-toilet platform his dad built in the family backyard, fully plumbed so every toilet can actually flush. Damian can point out each one's trapways, fill valves, siphon jets, and lid bolts. Then comes the flush.

Damian shares his collection on TikTok and Instagram, where hundreds of thousands of followers watch his videos. Brands even send him new models each week.

Skilled trades such as plumbing, carpentry, and welding need more young workers. A 2026 survey by the National Association of Home Builders found only 6 percent of young adults ages 18 to 25 planned to pursue a career in the construction trades. Yet between 2020 and 2025, enrollment in two-year trade schools grew by almost 20 percent. The nonprofit Bring Back the Trades says more than 1.4 million trade jobs will be vacant in 2030.

Roger, a trained carpenter, believes his son is headed for hands-on work. Right now, Damian says he wants to be a plumber, though his dad thinks he might become a toilet designer. Damian has been asking for a 3D printer so he can build his own toilets. His backup hobby is fixing washers and dryers.
why_it_matters: Skilled trades keep homes and buildings working, and the article shows how a fun hobby can point toward a real career that many employers will need.
